prompt.context: The Business Planning group at Stern Adventures, a leading amusement park located in Orlando that attracts 50 million people annually, must recommend to its CEO whether she should sign-off on a request to build a new ride for $300 million. Guests purchase a single ticket to experience all of the park's attractions. Currently, the market cannot support a rise in that ticket price as a means to cover the investment expense.
prompt.question: Should Business Planning recommend that the company's CEO sign-off on the $300 million capital request to build a new ride?

clarifying_info.q: What is the average admission revenue per person?
What is the average food and beverage revenue per person?
How many visitors does the park currently attract?
Can Stern Adventures raise the admission price?
clarifying_info.a: No. The Orlando theme park market is highly competitive; the park cannot raise the admission price.

clarifying_info.q: What is the expected attendance impact of opening a new ride of this magnitude?
clarifying_info.a: On average, Stern Adventures sees a 500,000 sustained increase in attendance when opening rides of this magnitude.

clarifying_info.q: What is the useful life of the ride?
clarifying_info.a: The attraction will be built to the highest specifications and should last more than 100 years; treat the investment as a perpetuity. Ignore capital maintenance issues.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should we use?
clarifying_info.a: Disney uses a discount rate of 10% for its theme parks business; use 10%.

framework: Determine incremental revenue generated by the new ride (additional visitors x revenue per visitor)
Calculate the present value of that perpetual incremental revenue stream using the given discount rate
Compute NPV by comparing PV of revenue to the $300 million investment cost
Assess strategic / qualitative benefits that may justify a negative-NPV project

questions.prompt: Calculate the annual incremental revenue from the new ride.
questions.guidance: Multiply the 500,000 additional guests by the total revenue per guest (admission + food & beverage). A strong answer recognizes that total per-guest spend includes both admission ($30) and food & beverage ($20).

math.setup: Additional guests x (admission revenue per guest + food & beverage revenue per guest)

questions.prompt: What is the present value of the incremental revenue stream?
questions.guidance: Since the ride is treated as a perpetuity (100+ year life), apply the perpetuity formula PV = Cash Flow / Discount Rate.

math.setup: PV of perpetuity = Annual cash flow / Discount rate

questions.prompt: What is the NPV of the investment, and what is your initial recommendation?
questions.guidance: NPV = PV of inflows minus initial investment. A negative NPV suggests the project destroys value on a pure financial basis; the candidate should clearly state this conclusion before pivoting to strategic considerations.

math.setup: NPV = PV of incremental revenue - Capital investment

questions.prompt: Despite the negative NPV, can you identify strategic reasons the park might still justify building the ride?
questions.guidance: Prompt the candidate to think beyond the pure financial model. Strong answers cover at least 2-3 of the categories below with concrete reasoning.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic benefits might justify building a ride that generates a negative NPV of -$50 million?

categories.name: Line Reduction / Guest Satisfaction
ideas: Lines at existing attractions will become shorter as guests are distributed across more attractions
Shorter wait times increase guest satisfaction, leading to positive word-of-mouth

categories.name: Extended Stay / In-Park Spend
ideas: More attractions give guests more reasons to stay longer on property
Longer dwell time increases opportunities for additional food, beverage, and merchandise purchases
Incremental spend from extended stays could offset some of the financial loss

categories.name: Wear-Out / Repeat Visitation
ideas: Guests need new incentives to return to a park they have already visited
A highly visible new attraction drives repeat visits and reduces guest 'wear-out'
Incremental revenue from returning guests not captured in the attendance model

recommendation: On a pure financial basis, the NPV is -$50 million ($250M PV of perpetuity minus $300M investment), so the project does not meet the financial hurdle rate

However, significant strategic benefits—line reduction, extended in-park spend, and repeat visitation—may justify the investment if management believes these effects are material enough to close the $50 million gap
risks: The 500,000 incremental visitors assumption may be optimistic; lower attendance uplift worsens the NPV further
Strategic benefits are difficult to quantify and may not materialize as expected
Competitive retaliation from other Orlando parks (e.g., Disney, Universal) could erode incremental attendance gains
next_steps: Quantify the incremental revenue from extended stays and repeat visits to assess whether they close the $50M shortfall
Conduct sensitivity analysis on the attendance uplift assumption
Benchmark against past Stern Adventures ride openings to validate the 500,000 uplift figure
